# Appendix A — The Grid {.unnumbered}

A gazetteer of the addresses and street names that carry the argument of this
book, with what happened at each and who it is named for.

Chapter V.11 makes the case that the street grid of the San Francisco Peninsula
is an accurate record of who controlled it and in what order. Chapter V.12 walks
the route. This appendix is the reference table both draw on, arranged in the
five layers that chapter V.11 identifies.

::: {.callout-note}
The author's street list has not yet been supplied. Every layer below is built to
receive additional names, and the argument rests on the pattern rather than on
any particular sign. Additions strengthen the appendix without altering the
chapter.
:::

## Layer one — the mission road (1769–1834)

| Name | What it is | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| El Camino Real | The Spanish supply route linking the missions a day's travel apart. Still the Peninsula's main street, running through Millbrae, San Mateo, Redwood City, Menlo Park, Palo Alto, Mountain View, and Sunnyvale. | II.2 |
| Junípero Serra Boulevard | Named for the Franciscan president of the mission system. Runs along the western edge of the Stanford campus. | II.1 |
| 320 Dolores Street, San Francisco | Mission San Francisco de Asís, founded 1776. Oldest intact building in the city; survived 1906. | II.1 |
| The Presidio, San Francisco | Spanish military anchor of the Bay, established 1776 within weeks of the mission. | II.2 |
| San Mateo, San Carlos, San Bruno, Santa Clara, San José | Mission and saint names that became the towns. | II.1 |

| Name | What it is | Chapter |
|---|---|---|
| Rancho San Francisquito | Mexican-era grant on the Peninsula; part of the land later assembled into the Stanford farm. | II.4 |
| Rancho de las Pulgas | Grant covering much of what is now San Mateo County; survives in road and place names. | II.4 |
| Rancho San Antonio, Corte Madera, and comparable names | Grant names persisting as neighbourhoods, roads, and open space preserves. | II.4 |
| Colton Hall, 570 Pacific Street, Monterey | California's constitutional convention, September–October 1849. Upper room preserved. | II.7 |

## The absences

Chapter V.11's sharpest section is the negative one. Set against the ledger in
chapter V.9, the record is as follows.

| Who | What is named for them on the Peninsula |
|---|---|
| The Muwekma Ohlone, whose territory the campus occupies | Very little; what exists is recent and small |
| The Chinese workforce of the Central Pacific | No major thoroughfare and no campus building. Commemorations are recent, modest, and largely the work of descendant organisations |
| The people sterilised under the 1909 law | Nothing |
| Farm workers | Cesar Chavez has streets and schools across California — a genuine and substantial exception, overwhelmingly in the Central Valley and in urban Latino neighbourhoods rather than here |
| Contract and platform workers | Nothing, and it is too early to expect anything |

What a place commemorates is what it has decided to remember. The list is the
argument.
